findings.title: Religious freedom and public-order limits
findings.assertion: Juárez's 4 December 1860 law protected Catholic worship and other religions, conditioned practice on the rights of others and public order, treated religious membership as voluntary, and removed civil sanctions for purely religious offenses such as apostasy or heresy.
findings.evidence_type: legislative text through edited modern transcription
findings.access_status: relevant articles examined; original printing not examined
limitations: editorial transcription needs comparison with 1860/1861 printed edition

findings.title: Church sanctuary and secular criminal justice
findings.assertion: The 1860 law abolished church sanctuary and permitted secular authorities to apprehend accused persons in temples under ordinary law without ecclesiastical control over their access; a rule, not evidence of a specific arrest.
findings.evidence_type: legislative text through edited modern transcription
findings.access_status: relevant articles examined; original printing not examined
limitations: editorial transcription needs comparison with 1860/1861 printed edition

findings.title: Civil oaths replaced by promises
findings.assertion: The 1860 law replaced obligatory religious oaths for officials, professions, testimony and certain declarations with explicit promises carrying legal consequences.
findings.evidence_type: legislative text through edited modern transcription
findings.access_status: relevant articles examined; original printing not examined
limitations: editorial transcription needs comparison with 1860/1861 printed edition

findings.title: Written permits for public religious processions
findings.assertion: The 1860 law required local political authorities' written permission for each solemn religious act outside temples and allowed permits to be withheld or activities stopped when disorder threatened; it does not establish any particular procession was banned.
findings.evidence_type: legislative text through edited modern transcription
findings.access_status: relevant articles examined; original printing not examined
limitations: editorial transcription needs comparison with 1860/1861 printed edition

findings.title: State control of the legal effects of marriage
findings.assertion: The 1860 law recognized freedom of religious marriage practice but assigned the marriage contract and its civil legal effects exclusively to secular law; lack of civil formalities prevented recognized civil effects.
findings.evidence_type: legislative text through edited modern transcription
findings.access_status: relevant articles examined; original printing not examined
limitations: editorial transcription needs comparison with 1860/1861 printed edition

findings.title: Cemetery access despite religious refusal
findings.assertion: Governors were instructed to enforce cemetery laws and guarantee dignified burial even if religious authorities refused religious services; no local enforcement outcomes were inspected.
findings.evidence_type: legislative text through edited modern transcription
findings.access_status: relevant articles examined; original printing not examined
limitations: editorial transcription needs comparison with 1860/1861 printed edition

findings.title: Officials' personal faith versus official attendance
findings.assertion: The 1860 law preserved individual religious freedom for public officials but barred their attendance in an official capacity at worship events, including formed troops.
findings.evidence_type: legislative text through edited modern transcription
findings.access_status: relevant articles examined; original printing not examined
limitations: editorial transcription needs comparison with 1860/1861 printed edition

findings.title: Civil takeover of ecclesiastical hospitals
findings.assertion: Juárez's 1861 decree secularized church-administered hospitals and charities, transferring direction and maintenance in the Federal District to the Union government and state establishments to oversight by the states. It does not prove any named hospital's implementation.
findings.evidence_type: legislative text through edited modern transcription
findings.access_status: relevant articles examined; original printing not examined
limitations: editorial transcription needs comparison with 1860/1861 printed edition

findings.title: Financial protections for secularized hospital assets
findings.assertion: The 1861 hospital decree kept estates, revenues and capital dedicated to the welfare establishments, preserved prior lawful property measures and regulated voluntary redemption/reinvestment of capital rather than simply ordering immediate liquidation.
findings.evidence_type: legislative text through edited modern transcription
